evidence_quotes.quote: The article summarizes policy challenges and solutions in the areas of water resource management and sustainable water supply and sanitation service provision.
but it is a myth that it is water scarcity that prevents universal access to drinking water. Once again, the problem is mostly rooted in governance and management.
Conversely, if tariff structures are not properly designed with social considerations, price increases may disproportionally affect poorer households.
For sanitation the situation is worse: between 1990 and 2006, the number of people without improved sanitation decreased from 2.6 billion to 2.5 billion.
Over the next couple of years, in the area of drinking water supply and sanitation, we at OECD will be working towards producing a “toolkit” for policy makers.

criterion_notes.c1: Sections 2, 4, and 5 explicitly address household/community drinking water supply and basic sanitation service access and affordability.
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording vs. narrow 2026-10-13 reading: Under the plain broad wording of Criterion 2, the paper touches on governance, institutional fragmentation across ministries, private sector participation, and consumer water tariffs/pricing (passing plain thematic mention). Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading, however, it fails (c2 = no) because it presents only unanalysed macro-governance background and high-level policy prescriptions rather than examining an operational rule-type mechanism (even where socially sensitive tariff structures are briefly mentioned in the abstract, no specific tariff rule or institutional mechanism is analysed). Under both readings, the overall decision remains exclude due to the complete absence of empirical evidence (E05).
criterion_notes.c3: This is an executive policy commentary/overview essay by the OECD Secretary-General with no primary data, no empirical methodology, no reference list, and no systematic empirical synthesis; it cites only headline secondary statistics (e.g., WHO-UNICEF MDG figures and OECD projections) to frame policy recommendations. Excluded under E05.
criterion_notes.c4: No empirical study outcome is measured or evaluated; the article only cites aggregate global descriptive figures (such as WHO-UNICEF global counts of people lacking improved water or sanitation) as background policy context.
criterion_notes.c5: Because this is a non-empirical policy essay, there is no identifiable empirical study design, study population/sample, unit of analysis, defined exposure, or measured outcome.
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is written in English.

country: Global / OECD and developing countries (mentions Australia, Chile, China, France, Japan, Korea, UK, and US only as illustrative examples)
rationale: Excluded as E05 (No empirical evidence). This 6-page article by OECD Secretary-General Angel Gurría is a high-level policy commentary and narrative overview summarizing global challenges in water resources management and water supply and sanitation financing/governance, concluding with an overview of upcoming OECD policy work. It contains no empirical research design, primary data collection, empirical socio-legal analysis, or systematic synthesis, and also provides only unanalysed macro-governance commentary rather than examining a specific rule-type mechanism governing household service access.
